analysis.one_liner: Sets new caps on power plant emissions of sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury through an expanded emissions-trading program.
analysis.headline: A Senate bill to cut power plant pollution was introduced in July 2002 and died in committee without a vote or a cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have replaced some Clean Air Act rules for coal-fired power plants with fixed annual caps on sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury, cutting each pollutant substantially from current levels. Power plants would have met the caps by trading emissions allowances, and units meeting the new standards would have been exempted from some permitting requirements for new or modified sources. It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: People living downwind of coal-fired power plants would gain cleaner air and lower exposure to acid rain, smog, and mercury. Merchants of the cleaner technologies, including natural gas generators and control-equipment makers, would gain demand.

how_it_helps.text: Sets declining annual tonnage limits for sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury from power plants, and makes the caps binding without regard to demand growth [S2].
Exempts units that meet the new performance standards from major-source permitting requirements that otherwise apply to construction and modification in polluted areas [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Owners of coal-fired power plants, which would have to install controls, buy allowances, or shift fuel; costs would tend to reach customers through electricity rates.

drawbacks.text: Exempting units from major-source review relaxes a safeguard that local communities currently use when new or modified plants are proposed in areas with unhealthy air [S2].
Allowance values depend on grandfathering based on historical fuel use, which favors incumbent large emitters relative to a full auction of the same cap [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cap would force real emissions cuts while keeping compliance flexible and capped in total, at the price of giving away much of the allowance value to incumbents and trimming permitting review for participating units.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee in July 2002 and never received any further action before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on July 29, 2002 and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S1].
The action record shows no further steps: no committee vote, no floor action, and no House action [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The power plants that would have faced the new caps and permitting pressure are better off; no one gained cleaner air, because the caps never took effect.

for.name: Bob Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks; it was referred to committee [S1].

sides.party_line_note: No votes were taken and no cosponsors signed on, so the partisan shape of support is not visible in the record [S4].

industries.note: Their sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury emissions would have been capped below current levels, forcing controls, fuel switches, or allowance purchases [S2].

industries.industry: Air pollution control equipment and cleaner generators
industries.note: Compliance demand for scrubbers, monitoring, and lower-emitting generation would rise under the caps [S2].
